candidates.userMessage: why does sqlite keep saying database is locked when it's just one process? I don't understand how locking works here
candidates.assistantExcerpt: Locked with a single process usually means there are more connections than you think, not that SQLite is broken. In the default rollback-journal mode a write takes an exclusive lock over the whole database file for the duration of the commit, so even a read opened at the wrong moment can collide with it. Your migration runner is the classic culprit: it opens its own connection, runs `BEGIN`, and if that transaction is still uncommitted when the application's connection tries to write, the second writer gets `SQLITE_BUSY`, which the driver surfaces as `database is locked`. One process, two connections, one transaction left open. The fix is two-fold. First, switch journal modes with `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;` - in write-ahead logging, readers get a snapshot of the database file while a single writer appends to the -wal file, so readers stop blocking the writer (there is still exactly one writer at a time, which is a SQLite invariant, not a mode setting). Second, set `busy_timeout` so a colliding writer waits a few seconds instead of failing immediately. And check for a leaked transaction: a `BEGIN` whose `COMMIT` was skipped by an early return holds the write lock until the connection closes. Rule of thumb: `database is locked` with one process means a connection you forgot about, so hunt for the second handle or the unfinished transaction before blaming SQLite.

The difference is when the expansion happens, and by whom. Inside double quotes, `"${DEPLOY_ENV}"` is expanded by the shell when it runs the script, because assignment and expansion happen left to right at execution time - so the value is whatever `DEPLOY_ENV` holds at that line, and it is missing from your log because the variable is set in the deploy job's environment but not exported, which means the child script never sees it. Inside single quotes nothing is expanded at all - the script literally contains the string `${DEPLOY_ENV}` and ssh or docker exec expands it on the far side. `set -x` in the log shows the pre-expansion text, so a single-quoted variable logs as its own name. Print the environment the script actually received with `env | grep DEPLOY` first; if it's absent there, the bug is in the caller's `export`, not in the quoting.

candidates.userMessage: what's a TIME_WAIT exactly? never heard that term
candidates.assistantExcerpt: When a TCP connection closes, the side that initiated the close keeps the socket in TIME_WAIT for 2*MSL - about 60 seconds on Linux - because segments already in flight could otherwise be delivered to a new connection reusing the same port, which means the kernel refuses to hand the same 4-tuple to a new listener while it is in that state. Servers opt out with `SO_REUSEADDR`, which lets a bind succeed over TIME_WAIT sockets. That is why an immediate restart of a server that just closed its listener can fail: the port is "in use" by a socket that isn't connected to anything. You can watch them accumulate with `netstat -an | grep TIME_WAIT` - a wall of them after a load test is normal, they drain on their own.

candidates.userMessage:
restart keeps failing with this:

Error: failed to bind to port 1420: EADDRINUSE address already in use

what does that actually mean? is it vite or the tauri shell holding it
candidates.assistantExcerpt: The error means the kernel still has a socket bound to port 1420 - nothing exotic, just a process that did not let go. Two usual suspects. First, the previous `pnpm tauri dev` did not fully die: the CLI kills the vite server, but a stale node or webkit process can hold the port for a moment after. Second, TIME_WAIT: when a TCP connection closes, the kernel keeps the connection state around for about 60 seconds so late packets can not corrupt a new connection on the same port, which means an immediate rebind of the same port can fail with EADDRINUSE even though nothing is listening. Find the holder with `lsof -i :1420` (or `ss -ltnp 'sport = :1420'`), kill that PID, and the restart works. Vite's dev server already sets `SO_REUSEADDR`, because a listening socket in TIME_WAIT is not really in use, so it lets the bind succeed - so when plain vite restarts cleanly, the port was free; when it doesn't, something is genuinely still alive. Rule of thumb: address already in use after a restart means something from the last run survived - check `lsof` before blaming the bundler.

The log line you pasted is the modem's response block, not an error: the firmware sends `AT+CGDCONT=1,"IP","hologram"` to define the PDP context - context ID 1, IPv4, APN "hologram" - and the modem answers `OK`. A block, in other words, is one AT command round-trip: a command line terminated by \r, then a final result code. If you're tracing why the modem is offline, the interesting part is which command came right before the failure, because the `AT+CGACT=1,1` further down the trace is what actually activates the context the CGDCONT line defined.

candidates.userMessage: why is useEffect running twice on mount? I thought it only re-runs when deps change
candidates.assistantExcerpt: The double run is React StrictMode doing its job, and only in development. In dev, StrictMode deliberately runs render twice and mounts, unmounts, and remounts every component once, because effects with missing cleanup produce real bugs that the double cycle makes impossible to miss: your `useEffect` runs, its cleanup runs, and it runs again. If the double invocation breaks your code, that is the bug surfacing, which means the effect was doing something it should have cleaned up - a fetch with no AbortController, a subscription never torn down, a timer never cleared. Production builds skip the double cycle entirely; the same component mounts once, so this never reaches users. The fix is not to remove `<React.StrictMode>` but to write the effect honestly: return a cleanup function that cancels the in-flight work, and make the effect idempotent so running it twice equals running it once. Rule of thumb: an effect that only works when it runs exactly once is a bug wearing a workaround.

candidates.userMessage: curl to the upstream works from my laptop but the service logs `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` in the container. not sure how the chain is supposed to get there
candidates.assistantExcerpt: The container doesn't trust the upstream's certificate because the Go binary, like every TLS client, verifies the server's chain against a local list of root certificates - and your base image doesn't have one. Your laptop works because macOS ships a system trust store that the Go runtime reads on its own; the minimal alpine image ships without `ca-certificates` on purpose, so `crypto/x509` finds no roots at `/etc/ssl/certs` and every chain fails as "signed by unknown authority", which means the fix is to install the bundle, not to disable verification. Add `apk add ca-certificates` in the Dockerfile and rebuild: the package generates `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`, a single concatenated PEM of Mozilla's root set, and Go picks it up through the system verifier with no code change. If the upstream's certificate is signed by a private CA - a corporate proxy or a self-managed intermediate - the public bundle won't contain that root, so you'd append the company root to the image's trust store and run `update-ca-certificates` in the build. Rule of thumb: "certificate signed by unknown authority" inside a container is a missing CA bundle nine times out of ten; check the image has `ca-certificates` before touching the Go code.

candidates.userMessage: why does it need the APN at all? I thought the SIM just connects like a phone
candidates.assistantExcerpt: An APN is the name of the carrier gateway a cellular data connection attaches to, and consumer SIMs ship with it baked in - the operator writes it onto the SIM profile during provisioning, so the phone never asks. IoT SIMs don't get that treatment: the carrier expects the device firmware to state the APN explicitly, which is why your modem sends `AT+CGDCONT=1,"IP","hologram"` before anything else - context ID 1, IPv4 PDP type, APN string. No APN means the modem registers on the network for SMS and voice but never opens a data bearer, because activating the PDP context with `AT+CGACT=1,1` fails when there is nothing defined to activate. The SIM identifies you to the network; the APN tells the network where your packets exit to the internet, which means a wrong APN gets you an IP on a gateway that won't route. Rule of thumb: SIM shows connected but no data means the APN was never set - check `AT+CGDCONT?` before anything else.

The migrations run on a separate connection from the pool, so they don't inherit `busy_timeout` - it is per-connection, not per-database. Run `PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000` on the migration connection too, or take the write lock explicitly with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` at the start of each migration so a collision fails fast instead of blocking. What you're seeing is the migration connection and the app connection fighting over the write lock at startup.
